Short definitions behind the underlined terms in the chapters: terms the text uses without developing, and recaps of ones it does develop, each linked back to its full treatment. Read it as a glossary or open entries in place from the text.

Hausdorff

A topological space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points p,qp, qp,q have disjoint open neighborhoods U∋pU \ni pU∋p, V∋qV \ni qV∋q with U∩V=∅U \cap V = \emptysetU∩V=∅. Most spaces appearing in differential geometry are Hausdorff: Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, every metric space, every — and every manifold, because the definition of a manifold demands it. The non-Hausdorff cases are exotic — the “line with two origins” is the canonical example.

Second countable

A topological space is second countable if its topology has a countable base: countably many open sets such that every open set is a union of some of them. For a metric space this is equivalent to having a countable dense subset: balls of rational radius about its points form a countable base. This is what makes and arguments work on a manifold.

Paracompact

A topological space is paracompact if every open cover admits a locally finite open refinement — a cover by smaller sets, each inside some original set, such that every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many of them. For manifolds the property comes for free: plus implies paracompact, and paracompactness is exactly what a needs to exist. It is the standard topological hypothesis under which the local-to-global constructions of differential geometry (gluing metrics, defining integration) go through.

Partition of unity

A partition of unity subordinate to an open cover {Uα}\{U_\alpha\}{Uα​} of MMM is a family of smooth functions ρα:M→[0,1]\rho_\alpha: M \to [0, 1]ρα​:M→[0,1], each supported inside the corresponding UαU_\alphaUα​, locally finite (every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports), with ∑αρα=1\sum_\alpha \rho_\alpha = 1∑α​ρα​=1 everywhere. On a smooth manifold every open cover admits one (this uses and the property). It turns local constructions into global ones: integration is defined chart by chart and glued (∫Mω=∑α∫ρα ω\int_M \tens{\omega} = \sum_\alpha \int \rho_\alpha\, \tens{\omega}∫M​ω=∑α​∫ρα​ω), Riemannian metrics are built by gluing chart-wise Euclidean ones, and local sections are extended globally.

Compact support

A function (or vector field, or differential form) has compact support if it vanishes outside some compact subset K⊆MK \subseteq MK⊆M. On a non-compact manifold this is the condition that makes ∫M\int_M∫M​ converge and that kills the boundary contributions at infinity — it is why Stokes’s theorem and the integration of nnn-forms are stated for compactly supported forms. On a compact manifold every smooth function has compact support automatically, so the qualifier can be dropped.

Embedded manifold

A smooth submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN is a subset M⊆RNM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NM⊆RN that is smoothly parametrized near each point: around every p∈Mp \in Mp∈M there is an open U⊆RNU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NU⊆RN, an open V⊆RnV \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nV⊆Rn, and a smooth map Φ:V→RN\Phi: V \to \mathbb{R}^NΦ:V→RN with everywhere-injective differential that is a homeomorphism onto U∩MU \cap MU∩M. The image Φ(V)\Phi(V)Φ(V) is an open piece of MMM, and the nnn coordinates on VVV are a chart on MMM.

The embedded view of differential geometry takes advantage of the ambient RN\mathbb{R}^NRN: tangent vectors are vectors in RN\mathbb{R}^NRN (spanning the tangent plane to MMM); the metric is the pullback of the Euclidean inner product; integration is over an embedded submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN. The Whitney embedding theorem says every smooth nnn-manifold can be embedded in R2n\mathbb{R}^{2n}R2n, so the embedded view loses no generality in principle. In practice the ambient space is excess baggage — isometric embeddings need many more dimensions (Nash), and a Lorentzian metric can only be induced from an indefinite-signature ambient space — which is why the abstract view is the working one.

Abstract manifold

An abstract smooth manifold is a , topological space equipped with an atlas of charts φα:Uα→Rn\varphi_\alpha: U_\alpha \to \mathbb{R}^nφα​:Uα​→Rn whose transition maps φβ∘φα−1\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}φβ​∘φα−1​ are smooth. No ambient space; the manifold is the chart-and-transition data, considered up to equivalence of atlases (equivalently, with a maximal atlas).

All structures — tangent spaces, tensor fields, metrics, connections — are then built intrinsically. The geometry in this book is mostly abstract, with the embedded view brought in as the geometrically transparent special case.

Chart

A chart (U,φ)(U, \varphi)(U,φ) is an open set U⊆MU \subseteq MU⊆M with a homeomorphism φ:U→φ(U)⊆Rn\varphi: U \to \varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nφ:U→φ(U)⊆Rn; its components xi=φix^i = \varphi^ixi=φi are local coordinates. Two charts are compatible when the transition map ψ∘φ−1\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}ψ∘φ−1 is a diffeomorphism on the overlap. A covering family of compatible charts is an atlas, and a maximal atlas is a smooth structure. Chapter 4 works with the inverse direction, the parametrization Φ=φ−1\Phi = \varphi^{-1}Φ=φ−1. Defined on the charts page.

Immersion

A smooth map F:M→NF: M \to NF:M→N is an immersion if its differential dFp:TpM→TF(p)NdF_p: T_p M \to T_{F(p)} NdFp​:Tp​M→TF(p)​N is injective at every point. (Compare: a submersion has surjective differential; an embedding is an injective immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image.) Immersions are the maps through which Riemannian metrics to metrics: for positive-definite g\tens{g}g, F∗gF^* \tens{g}F∗g is non-degenerate exactly when dFpdF_pdFp​ is injective. In indefinite signature injectivity is necessary but not sufficient — a null hyperplane in is embedded, yet its induced metric is degenerate. An immersion can self-intersect (a figure-eight curve in the plane); an cannot.

Derivation

For the commutative algebra A=C∞(M)A = C^\infty(M)A=C∞(M) of smooth functions on a manifold, a derivation at p∈Mp \in Mp∈M is an R\mathbb{R}R-linear map D:A→RD: A \to \mathbb{R}D:A→R satisfying the Leibniz rule

D(fg)=f(p) D(g)+g(p) D(f).D(fg) = f(p)\, D(g) + g(p)\, D(f). D(fg)=f(p)D(g)+g(p)D(f).

Every derivation at ppp is determined by its values on a coordinate system around ppp — D(xi)D(x^i)D(xi) for the chart x=(x1,…,xn)x = (x^1, \ldots, x^n)x=(x1,…,xn) — and the space of derivations is an nnn-dimensional real vector space, isomorphic to TpMT_p MTp​M.

The derivation viewpoint generalizes: a derivation of AAA (with values in AAA) is a vector field; the Lie bracket of vector fields is the commutator of derivations.

Musical isomorphism

The metric’s canonical identification of vectors with covectors. On a bare manifold the tangent space and its have the same dimension but no canonical isomorphism between them (contrast the double dual, where V∗∗≅VV^{**} \cong VV∗∗≅V is canonical). A metric g\tens{g}g provides one — the musical isomorphisms

♭:TpM→Tp∗M,v♭:=g(v,⋅),♯:=♭−1:Tp∗M→TpM,\flat: T_p M \to T^*_p M, \qquad \tens{v}^\flat := \tens{g}(\tens{v}, \cdot), \qquad \sharp := \flat^{-1}: T^*_p M \to T_p M, ♭:Tp​M→Tp∗​M,v♭:=g(v,⋅),♯:=♭−1:Tp∗​M→Tp​M,

named for how they move the component index down (vμ=gμν vνv_\mu = g_{\mu\nu}\, v^\nuvμ​=gμν​vν) and up (ωμ=gμν ων\omega^\mu = g^{\mu\nu}\, \omega_\nuωμ=gμνων​) — raising and lowering applied to a single index.

The gradient is the standard illustration of the distinction ♯\sharp♯ erases: the differential dfdfdf of a function is metric-free, but the gradient grad⁡f:=(df)♯\operatorname{grad} f := (df)^\sharpgradf:=(df)♯ is not. In Cartesian coordinates on Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn the two have identical components, which is why elementary vector calculus never distinguishes them; in any chart with gμν≠δμνg_{\mu\nu} \neq \delta_{\mu\nu}gμν​=δμν​ they differ.

Lie algebra

A Lie algebra over R\mathbb{R}R is a real vector space g\mathfrak{g}g equipped with a bilinear antisymmetric bracket [⋅,⋅]:g×g→g[\cdot, \cdot]: \mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}[⋅,⋅]:g×g→g satisfying the Jacobi identity

[X,[Y,Z]]+[Y,[Z,X]]+[Z,[X,Y]]=0.[\tens{X}, [\tens{Y}, \tens{Z}]] + [\tens{Y}, [\tens{Z}, \tens{X}]] + [\tens{Z}, [\tens{X}, \tens{Y}]] = 0. [X,[Y,Z]]+[Y,[Z,X]]+[Z,[X,Y]]=0.

Examples: gln(R)\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb{R})gln​(R) — n×nn \times nn×n real matrices with [A,B]=AB−BA[A, B] = AB - BA[A,B]=AB−BA; the tangent space at the identity of any ; the vector fields on a manifold under the Lie bracket. The vector-fields Lie algebra X(M)\mathfrak{X}(M)X(M) is infinite-dimensional and not the Lie algebra of any finite-dimensional Lie group.

Lie group

A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with multiplication and inversion smooth maps. Examples: GLn(R)GL_n(\mathbb{R})GLn​(R), the rotation groups SO(n)SO(n)SO(n), the Poincaré group of , Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn under addition, the circle S1S^1S1. The tangent space at the identity, with the bracket inherited from left-invariant vector fields, is the group’s . Isometry groups of pseudo-Riemannian manifolds are Lie groups — that is why counting counts a dimension.

A vector field whose flow is defined for all t∈Rt \in \mathbb{R}t∈R is complete; fields always are. Defined in full on the flows page.

Closed and exact forms

A form is closed if dω=0d\tens{\omega} = 0dω=0 and exact if ω=dη\tens{\omega} = d\tens{\eta}ω=dη. Every exact form is closed, because d2=0d^2 = 0d2=0. The converse holds locally (on sets, the Poincaré lemma) but fails globally. The standard example is (−y dx+x dy)/(x2+y2)(-y\, dx + x\, dy)/(x^2 + y^2)(−ydx+xdy)/(x2+y2) on the punctured plane, which integrates to 2π2\pi2π around the origin. The gap is measured by . Defined on the closed-and-exact page.

Orientation

An orientation of an nnn-manifold is a nowhere-vanishing nnn-form, taken up to multiplication by a positive function. A chart is positively oriented when dx1∧⋯∧dxndx^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^ndx1∧⋯∧dxn agrees with it. An orientation is what makes ∫Mω\int_M \tens{\omega}∫M​ω of an nnn-form well-defined: the change-of-variables Jacobian then always has positive sign. The Möbius strip and Klein bottle admit none. Defined on the integration page.

Stokes’s theorem

For an nnn-manifold MMM with boundary and a compactly supported (n−1)(n-1)(n−1)-form ω\tens{\omega}ω,

∫Mdω=∫∂Mω,\int_M d\tens{\omega} = \int_{\partial M} \tens{\omega}, ∫M​dω=∫∂M​ω,

with ∂M\partial M∂M given the outward-normal-first orientation. It contains the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green’s theorem, the classical Stokes theorem, and the divergence theorem. It also underlies integration by parts in every variational derivation. Defined on the Stokes page.

Configuration space

The configuration space QQQ of a mechanical system is the manifold of its possible positions, with holonomic constraints already enforced. Examples:

  • NNN free particles in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3: Q=R3NQ = \mathbb{R}^{3N}Q=R3N;
  • a pendulum: Q=S1Q = S^1Q=S1;
  • a rigid body: Q=R3×SO(3)Q = \mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3)Q=R3×SO(3), six-dimensional.

States live in the TQTQTQ (positions and velocities, Lagrangian mechanics) or the T∗QT^*QT∗Q (positions and momenta, Hamiltonian mechanics). Defined on the Newtonian-mechanics page.

Holonomic constraint

A constraint expressible as f(q,t)=0f(q, t) = 0f(q,t)=0 on configuration space. It restricts motion to a submanifold, which moves if fff depends on ttt. Examples: a rigid distance ∣rA−rB∣2−ℓ2=0\lvert \tens{r}_A - \tens{r}_B \rvert^2 - \ell^2 = 0∣rA​−rB​∣2−ℓ2=0, a bead on a wire, a particle on a surface. A constraint that involves velocities and is not integrable to a position constraint is nonholonomic. A disk rolling without slipping is the standard example: it restricts q˙\dot qq˙​ without reducing the dimension of QQQ. Treated on the constraints page.

Euler-Lagrange equations

The stationarity conditions of S=∫L(q,q˙,t) dtS = \int L(q, \dot q, t)\, dtS=∫L(q,q˙​,t)dt:

Noether’s theorem

If the flow of a vector field ξ\tens{\xi}ξ on QQQ leaves LLL invariant (or changes it by ddtF\tfrac{d}{dt}Fdtd​F), then

Tensor field

A tensor field of type (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) on a smooth manifold MMM is a smooth section of the bundle whose fiber at p∈Mp \in Mp∈M is

TpM⊗r⊗Tp∗M⊗s.T_p M^{\otimes r} \otimes T^*_p M^{\otimes s}. Tp​M⊗r⊗Tp∗​M⊗s.

Equivalently, a C∞(M)C^\infty(M)C∞(M)-multilinear map taking rrr smooth 111-forms and sss smooth vector fields and returning a smooth real-valued function. Vector fields are (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0)-tensor fields; 111-forms are (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1)-tensor fields; kkk-forms are alternating (0,k)(0, k)(0,k)-tensor fields; the metric is a symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor field. The Lie derivative and (given a connection) the covariant derivative extend to tensor fields of every type.

Einstein summation

The convention, due to Einstein and assumed tacitly wherever it is in force: a Greek (or Latin) index appearing exactly once up and exactly once down in the same monomial is summed over its range. So

vμωμ:=∑μvμωμ,Tμν Sνρ:=∑νTμν Sνρ.v^\mu \omega_\mu := \sum_{\mu} v^\mu \omega_\mu, \qquad T^\mu{}_\nu\, S^\nu{}_\rho := \sum_{\nu} T^\mu{}_\nu\, S^\nu{}_\rho. vμωμ​:=μ∑​vμωμ​,Tμν​Sνρ​:=ν∑​Tμν​Sνρ​.

Two ramifications. First, repeated indices in the same vertical position (vμωμv^\mu \omega^\muvμωμ, TμμT_{\mu\mu}Tμμ​) are almost always an error — there is no canonical pairing without a metric. Second, an index used as a dummy variable is bound and can be renamed: vμωμ=vνωνv^\mu \omega_\mu = v^\nu \omega_\nuvμωμ​=vνων​. Be wary of dummy collisions when chaining contractions.

Under a change of coordinates xμ↦x′μ′(x)x^\mu \mapsto x'^{\mu'}(x)xμ↦x′μ′(x), the components of an (r,s)(r, s)(r,s)-tensor transform as

Metric

A smooth symmetric non-degenerate (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)- g=gμν dxμ⊗dxν\tens{g} = g_{\mu\nu}\, dx^\mu \otimes dx^\nug=gμν​dxμ⊗dxν, with inverse gμνg^{\mu\nu}gμν (gμρgρν=δνμg^{\mu\rho} g_{\rho\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nugμρgρν​=δνμ​). Its signature is the numbers of positive and negative eigenvalues:

  • Lorentzian: (−,+,+,+)(-, +, +, +)(−,+,+,+) in this book; it adds the timelike / null / spacelike classification.

It supplies the , the , and the . Defined on the metric-tensor page.

Running example

The unit sphere

S2={(X,Y,Z)∈R3:X2+Y2+Z2=1}S^2 = \{ (X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1 \} S2={(X,Y,Z)∈R3:X2+Y2+Z2=1}

is the running example carried through Parts III–V of this book: charts, metric, curvature, and the mechanics of a particle and a pendulum on it. Two reasons it works:

  • Small enough to compute on by hand. Two coordinates, one round metric, four-line Christoffel calculation, single Riemann component.
  • Big enough to break intuition. Non-zero constant curvature; no global flat chart; non-trivial topology ( 222); SO(3)SO(3)SO(3) symmetry; closed orientable.

The drawback — S2S^2S2 is two-dimensional Riemannian, not four-dimensional Lorentzian — means it doesn’t model spacetime. But every tensor construction in the book is dimension- and signature-agnostic, so the formulas exercised on S2S^2S2 are the ones used on spacetime.

ω=∑μ1<⋯<μkωμ1⋯μk dxμ1∧⋯∧dxμk\tens{\omega} = \sum_{\mu_1 < \cdots < \mu_k} \omega_{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_k}\, dx^{\mu_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^{\mu_k} ω=μ1​<⋯<μk​∑​ωμ1​⋯μk​​dxμ1​∧⋯∧dxμk​

Levi-Civita

Three related but distinct objects share the name.

Levi-Civita symbol. The totally antisymmetric symbol εμ1⋯μn\varepsilon_{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_n}εμ1​⋯μn​​ — not a tensor — defined by ε1⋯n=1\varepsilon_{1 \cdots n} = 1ε1⋯n​=1 and antisymmetry under any pair swap. Coordinate-dependent: it transforms like a of weight +1+1+1. Used in the explicit formula for the Hodge star.

Levi-Civita connection. The unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M, \tens{g})(M,g) — the connection assumed throughout standard GR. Its Christoffel symbols are

Γρμν=12 gρσ(∂μgνσ+∂νgσμ−∂σgμν),\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{\rho\sigma} \left( \partial_\mu g_{\nu\sigma} + \partial_\nu g_{\sigma\mu} - \partial_\sigma g_{\mu\nu} \right), Γρμν​=21​gρσ(∂μ​gνσ​+∂ν​gσμ​−∂σ​gμν​),

derived on the covariant-derivative page.

Three different objects, one Italian mathematician. Context picks which is meant.

Tensor density

A tensor density of weight www is a component array that transforms by the times an extra factor [det⁡(∂x′/∂x)]w\bigl[\det(\partial x'/\partial x)\bigr]^w[det(∂x′/∂x)]w of the Jacobian determinant. Weight 000 is an ordinary tensor. The symbol (lower indices) has weight +1+1+1; ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ is a scalar density of weight −1-1−1; their product is an honest tensor — the general pattern, since multiplying by the appropriate power of ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ converts any density to a tensor. Densities appear wherever determinants do: volume elements, integrands, and the ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ factors of the variational formulas in chapter 15. (Sign conventions for www vary across textbooks — some count powers of det⁡(∂x/∂x′)\det(\partial x/\partial x')det(∂x/∂x′) instead.)

Geodesic

A curve whose velocity is along itself:

∇γ˙γ˙=0,in coordinatesγ¨ρ+Γρμν γ˙μγ˙ν=0.\nabla_{\dot\gamma} \dot\gamma = 0, \qquad \text{in coordinates} \quad \ddot\gamma^\rho + \Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu}\, \dot\gamma^\mu \dot\gamma^\nu = 0. ∇γ˙​​γ˙​=0,in coordinatesγ¨​ρ+Γρμν​γ˙​μγ˙​ν=0.

Minkowski space

The spacetime of special relativity: R4\mathbb{R}^4R4 with the global flat Lorentzian metric

η=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2\tens{\eta} = -dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 η=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2

(signature (−,+,+,+)(-, +, +, +)(−,+,+,+)). All Christoffel symbols vanish in these coordinates, so are straight lines and the Riemann tensor is zero — the “no gravity” special case that curved solutions approach asymptotically (Schwarzschild as r→∞r \to \inftyr→∞). Its group is the Poincaré group: translations plus Lorentz transformations. Every tangent space of a Lorentzian manifold is a copy of Minkowski space in miniature (causal structure).

Lovelock’s theorem

In four dimensions, every symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor that is (i) built from the metric and at most its first and second derivatives and (ii) divergence-free is a linear combination

a Gμν+b gμνa\, G_{\mu\nu} + b\, g_{\mu\nu} aGμν​+bgμν​

of the Einstein tensor and the metric. So the left-hand side of the Einstein equations — including the cosmological-constant term — is forced, not chosen, once a tensorial second-order theory of the metric is demanded. In dimension n>4n > 4n>4, additional “Lovelock terms” (Gauss–Bonnet and higher) become available, which is one reason higher-dimensional gravity theories are less rigid than $4$D GR.

Cartan formalism

The tetrad (or vielbein) formulation of gravity. Replace the coordinate basis with an orthonormal coframe: nnn one-forms eae^aea with

g=ηab  ea⊗eb,\tens{g} = \eta_{ab}\; e^a \otimes e^b, g=ηab​ea⊗eb,

where η\tens{\eta}η is the flat metric of the appropriate signature (“tetrad” when n=4n = 4n=4). The connection becomes the spin connection ωab\omega^a{}_bωab​, a matrix of one-forms, and torsion and curvature become the two-forms of the Cartan structure equations

Ta=dea+ωab∧eb,Rab=dωab+ωac∧ωcb.T^a = de^a + \omega^a{}_b \wedge e^b, \qquad R^a{}_b = d\omega^a{}_b + \omega^a{}_c \wedge \omega^c{}_b. Ta=dea+ωab​∧eb,Rab​=dωab​+ωac​∧ωcb​.

The payoff: fields on curved spacetime become definable (spinors transform under local frame rotations, which the coordinate-basis formalism has no handle on), and the Einstein–Cartan action becomes a polynomial in differential forms. Misner–Thorne–Wheeler (chapter 13) and Nakahara develop the formalism in full.

Spinor

A field that transforms under the Spin group — the double cover of the rotation group SO(n)SO(n)SO(n) (or, in Lorentzian signature, of the Lorentz group) — rather than under the group itself. The double-cover subtlety is physical: a spinor changes sign under a 2π2\pi2π rotation and returns to itself only after 4π4\pi4π. Electrons, quarks, and all Standard-Model fermions are described by (Dirac) spinors. Spin representations do not extend to GLnGL_nGLn​, so spinors cannot be defined from a coordinate basis alone — curved-spacetime spinors need an orthonormal frame and spin connection (the ). Their intrinsic angular momentum is the spin density that sources torsion in Einstein–Cartan gravity.

Contractible

Two smooth maps F,G:M→NF, G: M \to NF,G:M→N are (smoothly) homotopic, written F≃GF \simeq GF≃G, if one can be deformed into the other: there is a smooth H:M×[0,1]→NH: M \times [0, 1] \to NH:M×[0,1]→N with H(⋅,0)=FH(\cdot, 0) = FH(⋅,0)=F and H(⋅,1)=GH(\cdot, 1) = GH(⋅,1)=G. A manifold MMM is contractible if its identity map is homotopic to a constant map — MMM can be continuously shrunk to a point. Convex and subsets of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn are contractible; Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn is, but Rn∖{0}\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}Rn∖{0} and the sphere are not.

De Rham cohomology is a homotopy invariant: homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology, so a contractible manifold has the cohomology of a point (all reduced groups vanish — the Poincaré lemma).

Lie group

A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with multiplication and inversion smooth maps. Examples: GLn(R)GL_n(\mathbb{R})GLn​(R), the rotation groups SO(n)SO(n)SO(n), the Poincaré group of , Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn under addition, the circle S1S^1S1. The tangent space at the identity, with the bracket inherited from left-invariant vector fields, is the group’s . Isometry groups of pseudo-Riemannian manifolds are Lie groups — that is why counting counts a dimension.

Paracompact

A topological space is paracompact if every open cover admits a locally finite open refinement — a cover by smaller sets, each inside some original set, such that every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many of them. For manifolds the property comes for free: plus implies paracompact, and paracompactness is exactly what a needs to exist. It is the standard topological hypothesis under which the local-to-global constructions of differential geometry (gluing metrics, defining integration) go through.

Partition of unity

A partition of unity subordinate to an open cover {Uα}\{U_\alpha\}{Uα​} of MMM is a family of smooth functions ρα:M→[0,1]\rho_\alpha: M \to [0, 1]ρα​:M→[0,1], each supported inside the corresponding UαU_\alphaUα​, locally finite (every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many supports), with ∑αρα=1\sum_\alpha \rho_\alpha = 1∑α​ρα​=1 everywhere. On a smooth manifold every open cover admits one (this uses and the property). It turns local constructions into global ones: integration is defined chart by chart and glued (∫Mω=∑α∫ρα ω\int_M \tens{\omega} = \sum_\alpha \int \rho_\alpha\, \tens{\omega}∫M​ω=∑α​∫ρα​ω), Riemannian metrics are built by gluing chart-wise Euclidean ones, and local sections are extended globally.

Second countable

A topological space is second countable if its topology has a countable base: countably many open sets such that every open set is a union of some of them. For a metric space this is equivalent to having a countable dense subset: balls of rational radius about its points form a countable base. This is what makes and arguments work on a manifold.

Hausdorff

A topological space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points p,qp, qp,q have disjoint open neighborhoods U∋pU \ni pU∋p, V∋qV \ni qV∋q with U∩V=∅U \cap V = \emptysetU∩V=∅. Most spaces appearing in differential geometry are Hausdorff: Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, every metric space, every — and every manifold, because the definition of a manifold demands it. The non-Hausdorff cases are exotic — the “line with two origins” is the canonical example.

Embedded manifold

A smooth submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN is a subset M⊆RNM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NM⊆RN that is smoothly parametrized near each point: around every p∈Mp \in Mp∈M there is an open U⊆RNU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^NU⊆RN, an open V⊆RnV \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nV⊆Rn, and a smooth map Φ:V→RN\Phi: V \to \mathbb{R}^NΦ:V→RN with everywhere-injective differential that is a homeomorphism onto U∩MU \cap MU∩M. The image Φ(V)\Phi(V)Φ(V) is an open piece of MMM, and the nnn coordinates on VVV are a chart on MMM.

The embedded view of differential geometry takes advantage of the ambient RN\mathbb{R}^NRN: tangent vectors are vectors in RN\mathbb{R}^NRN (spanning the tangent plane to MMM); the metric is the pullback of the Euclidean inner product; integration is over an embedded submanifold of RN\mathbb{R}^NRN. The Whitney embedding theorem says every smooth nnn-manifold can be embedded in R2n\mathbb{R}^{2n}R2n, so the embedded view loses no generality in principle. In practice the ambient space is excess baggage — isometric embeddings need many more dimensions (Nash), and a Lorentzian metric can only be induced from an indefinite-signature ambient space — which is why the abstract view is the working one.

A function (or vector field, or differential form) has compact support if it vanishes outside some compact subset K⊆MK \subseteq MK⊆M. On a compact manifold every smooth function has compact support automatically, so the qualifier can be dropped.

Tensor field

A tensor field of type (r,s)(r, s)(r,s) on a smooth manifold MMM is a smooth section of the bundle whose fiber at p∈Mp \in Mp∈M is

TpM⊗r⊗Tp∗M⊗s.T_p M^{\otimes r} \otimes T^*_p M^{\otimes s}. Tp​M⊗r⊗Tp∗​M⊗s.

Equivalently, a C∞(M)C^\infty(M)C∞(M)-multilinear map taking rrr smooth 111-forms and sss smooth vector fields and returning a smooth real-valued function. Vector fields are (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0)-tensor fields; 111-forms are (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1)-tensor fields; kkk-forms are alternating (0,k)(0, k)(0,k)-tensor fields; the metric is a symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor field. The Lie derivative and (given a connection) the covariant derivative extend to tensor fields of every type.

Contractible

Two smooth maps F,G:M→NF, G: M \to NF,G:M→N are (smoothly) homotopic, written F≃GF \simeq GF≃G, if one can be deformed into the other: there is a smooth H:M×[0,1]→NH: M \times [0, 1] \to NH:M×[0,1]→N with H(⋅,0)=FH(\cdot, 0) = FH(⋅,0)=F and H(⋅,1)=GH(\cdot, 1) = GH(⋅,1)=G. A manifold MMM is contractible if its identity map is homotopic to a constant map — MMM can be continuously shrunk to a point. Convex and subsets of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn are contractible; Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn is, but Rn∖{0}\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}Rn∖{0} and the sphere are not.

De Rham cohomology is a homotopy invariant: homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology, so a contractible manifold has the cohomology of a point (all reduced groups vanish — the Poincaré lemma).

Orientation

An orientation of an nnn-manifold is a nowhere-vanishing nnn-form, taken up to multiplication by a positive function. A chart is positively oriented when dx1∧⋯∧dxndx^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dx^ndx1∧⋯∧dxn agrees with it. An orientation is what makes ∫Mω\int_M \tens{\omega}∫M​ω of an nnn-form well-defined: the change-of-variables Jacobian then always has positive sign. The Möbius strip and Klein bottle admit none. Defined on the integration page.

Γρμν=12 gρσ(∂μgνσ+∂νgσμ−∂σgμν),\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{\rho\sigma} \left( \partial_\mu g_{\nu\sigma} + \partial_\nu g_{\sigma\mu} - \partial_\sigma g_{\mu\nu} \right), Γρμν​=21​gρσ(∂μ​gνσ​+∂ν​gσμ​−∂σ​gμν​),

Tensor density

A tensor density of weight www is a component array that transforms by the times an extra factor [det⁡(∂x′/∂x)]w\bigl[\det(\partial x'/\partial x)\bigr]^w[det(∂x′/∂x)]w of the Jacobian determinant. Weight 000 is an ordinary tensor. The symbol (lower indices) has weight +1+1+1; ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ is a scalar density of weight −1-1−1; their product is an honest tensor — the general pattern, since multiplying by the appropriate power of ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ converts any density to a tensor. Densities appear wherever determinants do: volume elements, integrands, and the ∣det⁡g∣\sqrt{|\det g|}∣detg∣​ factors of the variational formulas in chapter 15. (Sign conventions for www vary across textbooks — some count powers of det⁡(∂x/∂x′)\det(\partial x/\partial x')det(∂x/∂x′) instead.)

For the Levi-Civita connection they are the critical curves of length: great circles on the sphere, straight lines in flat space. In GR, timelike geodesics are the worldlines of free-falling massive particles and null geodesics the worldlines of light. Along any geodesic, each ξ\tens{\xi}ξ gives a conserved quantity ξμγ˙μ\xi_\mu \dot\gamma^\muξμ​γ˙​μ. Developed on the covariant-derivative page.

Stress-energy tensor

The symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor TμνT_{\mu\nu}Tμν​ of matter and non-gravitational fields. Its components give energy density (T00T_{00}T00​), momentum density, and stress. For a perfect fluid, Tμν=(ρ+p) uμuν+p gμνT_{\mu\nu} = (\rho + p)\, u_\mu u_\nu + p\, g_{\mu\nu}Tμν​=(ρ+p)uμ​uν​+pgμν​. Lovelock's theorem

In four dimensions, every symmetric (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2)-tensor that is (i) built from the metric and at most its first and second derivatives and (ii) divergence-free is a linear combination

a Gμν+b gμνa\, G_{\mu\nu} + b\, g_{\mu\nu} aGμν​+bgμν​

of the Einstein tensor and the metric. So the left-hand side of the Einstein equations — including the cosmological-constant term — is forced, not chosen, once a tensorial second-order theory of the metric is demanded. In dimension n>4n > 4n>4, additional “Lovelock terms” (Gauss–Bonnet and higher) become available, which is one reason higher-dimensional gravity theories are less rigid than $4$D GR.

Spinor

A field that transforms under the Spin group — the double cover of the rotation group SO(n)SO(n)SO(n) (or, in Lorentzian signature, of the Lorentz group) — rather than under the group itself. The double-cover subtlety is physical: a spinor changes sign under a 2π2\pi2π rotation and returns to itself only after 4π4\pi4π. Electrons, quarks, and all Standard-Model fermions are described by (Dirac) spinors. Spin representations do not extend to GLnGL_nGLn​, so spinors cannot be defined from a coordinate basis alone — curved-spacetime spinors need an orthonormal frame and spin connection (the ). Their intrinsic angular momentum is the spin density that sources torsion in Einstein–Cartan gravity.

Cartan formalism

The tetrad (or vielbein) formulation of gravity. Replace the coordinate basis with an orthonormal coframe: nnn one-forms eae^aea with

g=ηab  ea⊗eb,\tens{g} = \eta_{ab}\; e^a \otimes e^b, g=ηab​ea⊗eb,

where η\tens{\eta}η is the flat metric of the appropriate signature (“tetrad” when n=4n = 4n=4). The connection becomes the spin connection ωab\omega^a{}_bωab​, a matrix of one-forms, and torsion and curvature become the two-forms of the Cartan structure equations

Ta=dea+ωab∧eb,Rab=dωab+ωac∧ωcb.T^a = de^a + \omega^a{}_b \wedge e^b, \qquad R^a{}_b = d\omega^a{}_b + \omega^a{}_c \wedge \omega^c{}_b. Ta=dea+ωab​∧eb,Rab​=dωab​+ωac​∧ωcb​.

The payoff: fields on curved spacetime become definable (spinors transform under local frame rotations, which the coordinate-basis formalism has no handle on), and the Einstein–Cartan action becomes a polynomial in differential forms. Misner–Thorne–Wheeler (chapter 13) and Nakahara develop the formalism in full.

Cochain complex

A cochain complex is a sequence of abelian groups (or vector spaces) and linear maps

⋯→Ck−1→dk−1Ck→dkCk+1→⋯\cdots \to C^{k-1} \xrightarrow{d^{k-1}} C^k \xrightarrow{d^k} C^{k+1} \to \cdots ⋯→Ck−1dk−1​Ckdk​Ck+1→⋯

with dk∘dk−1=0d^k \circ d^{k-1} = 0dk∘dk−1=0 for every kkk. The kernel of each dkd^kdk (“cocycles”) contains the image of the previous dk−1d^{k-1}dk−1 (“coboundaries”), and the quotient ker⁡(dk)/im(dk−1)\ker(d^k) / \mathrm{im}(d^{k-1})ker(dk)/im(dk−1) is the kkk-th cohomology of the complex. The complex Ω0→Ω1→Ω2→⋯\Omega^0 \to \Omega^1 \to \Omega^2 \to \cdotsΩ0→Ω1→Ω2→⋯ with exterior derivative as ddd is the de Rham complex.

A chain complex is the same structure with the maps lowering degree (∂k:Ck→Ck−1\partial_k: C_k \to C_{k-1}∂k​:Ck​→Ck−1​, ∂2=0\partial^2 = 0∂2=0); its quotients are homology. Dualizing a chain complex — Ck:=Hom(Ck,A)C^k := \mathrm{Hom}(C_k, A)Ck:=Hom(Ck​,A) with d:=∂∗d := \partial^*d:=∂∗ — produces a cochain complex, which is exactly how arises from the singular chain complex.

Star-shaped

An open set U⊆RnU \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nU⊆Rn is star-shaped about p∈Up \in Up∈U if for every q∈Uq \in Uq∈U, the line segment {(1−t)p+tq:t∈[0,1]}\{(1-t)p + tq : t \in [0, 1]\}{(1−t)p+tq:t∈[0,1]} from ppp to qqq lies entirely in UUU. Convex sets are star-shaped about any of their points. Star-shaped sets are contractible — the homotopy H(q,t)=(1−t)q+tpH(q, t) = (1-t)q + tpH(q,t)=(1−t)q+tp retracts UUU to ppp — and this contraction is the ingredient that makes the cone-operator proof of the Poincaré lemma work.
